body:
Political background

In the early 16th century, northern India was ruled from Delhi by the Lodi dynasty, the last ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. Ibrahim Lodi was its ruler when Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur advanced into northern India from Kabul.

Babur had established himself in Kabul in 1504. His campaign against Ibrahim Lodi brought him into direct conflict with the political power controlling Delhi and Agra. The result was the First Battle of Panipat, fought on 21 April 1526 near Panipat in present-day Haryana.

The opposing sides and result

  • Babur: Invading ruler based in Kabul and founder of the Mughal dynasty in India.
  • Ibrahim Lodi: Sultan of Delhi and ruler of the Lodi dynasty.
  • Winner: Babur.
  • Immediate result: Ibrahim Lodi was killed, Lodi rule at Delhi ended, and Babur occupied Delhi and Agra.

Why Babur's army succeeded

Babur combined cavalry with effective use of firearms and field artillery. His forces used defensive arrangements involving carts and guns, while mobile cavalry supported attacks against the opposing army. The coordinated use of these forces contributed to his victory.

The battle is particularly associated with the importance of artillery in early Mughal warfare. However, gunpowder and firearms were not introduced into India for the first time by Babur. Gunpowder technology had entered Indian warfare earlier, and firearms had already been used in regions including Gujarat, Malwa and the Deccan. What distinguished Panipat was Babur's effective employment of artillery in a major battle for Delhi.

What the victory established

The victory marked the beginning of Mughal rule in India. It gave Babur control of the major political centres of Delhi and Agra, but it did not mean that every regional ruler accepted his authority. The Rajput powers and Afghan opponents continued to challenge the new Mughal position. Babur's campaigns at Khanwa, Chanderi and Ghaghra followed.

Prelims focus

  • Date: 21 April 1526.
  • Opponents: Babur and Ibrahim Lodi.
  • Place: Panipat, in present-day Haryana.
  • Result: Babur won; Ibrahim Lodi was killed.
  • Significance: Beginning of Mughal rule at Delhi and Agra.
  • Trap: Babur used artillery effectively, but he was not the first person to introduce gunpowder into Indian warfare.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, printed pp. 47–48, 2020–21 edition; Panipat District Administration, First Battle of Panipat (1526), consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Artistic reconstruction of an early Mughal battlefield in 1526.

pictures.alt: Babur’s victory on 21 April 1526 brought Delhi and Agra under his control, while Rajput and Afghan opposition meant consolidation remained ahead.

title: First Battle of Panipat (1526): The Beginning of Mughal Rule

body:
Why further battles followed Panipat

The defeat of Ibrahim Lodi gave Babur control of Delhi and Agra, but important regional powers remained outside his authority. He faced resistance from Rajput rulers in northwestern and central India and from Afghan leaders who continued to contest Mughal expansion.

Three campaigns are particularly important for understanding how Babur consolidated his position after 1526: Khanwa in 1527, Chanderi in 1528 and Ghaghra in 1529. They involved different opponents and should not be treated as repeated battles against the same army.

Battle of Khanwa, 1527

The Battle of Khanwa was fought in 1527 near Khanwa in present-day Rajasthan. Babur faced a coalition led by Rana Sanga, also known as Sangram Singh, the ruler of Mewar. Rana Sanga's forces included Rajput rulers and their allies.

Babur won the battle. The defeat weakened the coalition that had challenged his authority in northern India. Khanwa was especially important because Babur's opponent was a major Rajput ruler rather than the Delhi Sultan he had defeated at Panipat.

Battle of Chanderi, 1528

In 1528, Babur attacked Chanderi in present-day Madhya Pradesh. The fort was held by Medini Rai, a Rajput chief associated with resistance to Babur.

Babur captured Chanderi. The campaign reduced an important centre of Rajput opposition in central India. Although Khanwa and Chanderi were both Mughal victories against Rajput opponents, they occurred in different years and involved different principal leaders.

Battle of Ghaghra, 1529

In 1529, Babur fought against eastern Afghan opponents, particularly forces associated with Mahmud Lodi. The fighting occurred near the confluence of the Ghaghra and Ganga rivers. The Bengal Sultanate under Nusrat Shah was also involved in the wider confrontation.

Babur emerged victorious and secured his position against an important eastern challenge. The campaign was followed by a peace agreement with Bengal. It should not be described as Babur's complete conquest of the Bengal Sultanate.

Three battles, three different immediate objectives

At Khanwa, Babur faced a powerful Rajput coalition. At Chanderi, he attacked a fortified centre of Rajput resistance. At Ghaghra, he confronted Afghan forces operating in the east. Together, these campaigns strengthened the Mughal position established at Panipat, but each had a distinct opponent and geographical setting.

Prelims focus

  • Khanwa, 1527: Babur defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar and his allies.
  • Chanderi, 1528: Babur defeated Medini Rai and captured the fort.
  • Ghaghra, 1529: Babur defeated eastern Afghan opponents associated with Mahmud Lodi.
  • Geographical distinction: Khanwa is in Rajasthan; Chanderi is in Madhya Pradesh; Ghaghra was fought near the Ganga–Ghaghra river confluence.
  • Trap: The Battle of Khanwa was not fought against Ibrahim Lodi. Ibrahim Lodi had already been defeated at Panipat in 1526.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, printed p. 48, 2020–21 edition; Babur, Memoirs, Volume 2, account of the Chanderi campaign of 1528, online translation consulted 19 November 2026; History of War, Battle of the Gogra River, 1529, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: After defeating Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat, Babur faced Rana Sanga at Khanwa, Medini Rai at Chanderi, and Mahmud Lodi’s eastern Afghan opponents at Ghaghra.
pictures.caption: Babur's campaigns after Panipat challenged different regional opponents.

title: Khanwa, Chanderi and Ghaghra (1527–1529): Babur Consolidates His Position

body:
Humayun faces an Afghan challenge

Babur was succeeded by his son Humayun in 1530. Mughal control was still relatively new, and Afghan leaders continued to compete for power. The most successful challenger was Sher Khan, who later ruled as Sher Shah Suri.

Two defeats forced Humayun out of northern India. These events explain why the Mughal dynasty established by Babur in 1526 did not maintain uninterrupted control of Delhi during the following decades.

Battle of Chausa, 1539

The Battle of Chausa was fought in 1539 near Chausa in present-day Bihar. Sher Khan defeated Humayun. The victory greatly strengthened Sher Khan's position and weakened Mughal authority in northern India.

Battle of Kannauj, 1540

The following year, in 1540, Sher Shah defeated Humayun again at the Battle of Kannauj, also called the Battle of Bilgram. This defeat forced Humayun to leave his kingdom. The Sur dynasty replaced Mughal rule at Delhi.

The distinction between the 2 battles is straightforward: Chausa, 1539, was the first major defeat; Kannauj, 1540, resulted in Humayun losing control of the empire.

Humayun returns in 1555

Humayun regained Delhi in 1555 after a period of exile and military recovery. However, he died in 1556. His young son Akbar became emperor, with Bairam Khan acting as his guardian and regent.

At this time, Mughal control remained vulnerable. Hemu, also known as Hem Chandra Vikramaditya, had risen through the administration and military leadership of the Sur establishment. He defeated Mughal forces and occupied Delhi, creating another challenge to Mughal rule.

Second Battle of Panipat, 1556

The Second Battle of Panipat was fought on 5 November 1556 between Hemu's army and the forces of the young emperor Akbar. Bairam Khan directed the Mughal response, while Mughal generals commanded the troops in the battle.

Hemu personally led his forces and was seriously wounded during the fighting. His army was subsequently defeated. The Mughal victory restored Akbar's position in Delhi and helped establish the foundation for the later expansion of his empire.

Akbar was the Mughal emperor in 1556, but he was only 14 years old at the battle. The Second Battle of Panipat should therefore not be described as a personal battlefield duel between Akbar and Hemu.

How the sequence fits together

The years 1539, 1540, 1555 and 1556 describe different stages of the struggle for Delhi: Humayun's defeat, loss of his kingdom, recovery of the capital and the successful defence of Akbar's claim against Hemu.

Prelims focus

  • Chausa, 1539: Sher Khan defeated Humayun.
  • Kannauj or Bilgram, 1540: Sher Shah defeated Humayun, ending the first phase of Humayun's rule.
  • 1555: Humayun regained Delhi.
  • Second Panipat, 5 November 1556: Akbar's forces defeated Hemu.
  • Regent: Bairam Khan acted for the young Akbar.
  • Trap: Chausa and Kannauj were victories of Sher Khan or Sher Shah, whereas the Second Battle of Panipat was a Mughal victory against Hemu.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, printed pp. 48–49, 2020–21 edition; Panipat District Administration, Second Battle of Panipat (1556), consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline showing Humayun’s defeats in 1539 and 1540, recovery of Delhi in 1555, and Akbar’s succession and forces’ victory over Hemu in 1556.
pictures.caption: The loss, recovery and defence of Mughal authority from 1539 to 1556.

title: Chausa, Kannauj and Second Panipat (1539–1556): Loss and Recovery of Mughal Rule

body:
Vijayanagara and the Deccan Sultanates

The Vijayanagara Empire was a major power in southern India, with its capital at Vijayanagara, whose remains are associated with present-day Hampi in Karnataka. Its rulers competed with the Deccan Sultanates for territory, influence and resources, especially in the region between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.

Relations between Vijayanagara and the Sultanates were not permanently hostile. Alliances changed according to political circumstances. At times, Vijayanagara intervened in conflicts among the Sultanates, while the Sultanates also took part in the politics of Vijayanagara.

Who fought at Talikota?

The Battle of Talikota was fought in 1565. It is also known as the Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi.

  • Vijayanagara side: Forces led by Rama Raya, the powerful chief minister and effective political leader of the empire.
  • Opposing side: A coalition of Deccan Sultanates. The principal armies identified in NCERT were those of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda.
  • Result: The combined Sultanate forces defeated the Vijayanagara army. Rama Raya was killed during the conflict.

Some historical accounts also include Bidar among the allied Sultanates. This should not be confused with the claim that all 5 Deccan Sultanates necessarily contributed equally to the battle. The central fact remains that a coalition of Sultanate forces defeated Vijayanagara.

Why the defeat was important

The victorious armies subsequently attacked and sacked the city of Vijayanagara. The capital suffered severe destruction and was largely abandoned within a few years. Its former importance as an imperial capital came to an end.

Did the empire disappear immediately?

The fall of the capital and the complete disappearance of the empire were not the same event. After 1565, the surviving political leadership continued under the Aravidu dynasty, with centres of power farther east. Penukonda and later Chandragiri became important seats of the reduced kingdom.

Thus, the battle destroyed the political and economic dominance of the old capital, but some elements of Vijayanagara rule continued elsewhere.

Prelims focus

  • Year: 1565.
  • Other name: Rakshasi-Tangadi.
  • Vijayanagara leader: Rama Raya.
  • Opponents: A coalition principally associated with Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda.
  • Result: Vijayanagara was defeated; its capital was later sacked.
  • Trap: The destruction of the capital did not mean that every successor of Vijayanagara immediately ceased to rule.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part II, Class 12, Theme 7, An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara, printed pp. 172–174; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 6, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, printed p. 84; Emma J. Flatt, The Courts of the Deccan Sultanates, Introduction, Historical Background, p. 9, Cambridge University Press.]

pictures.alt: Residents carrying bundles leave damaged Vijayanagara streets, with stone ruins, temple towers and Hampi's rocky hills behind them.
pictures.caption: Artistic reconstruction of the damaged Vijayanagara capital after the defeat of 1565.

pictures.alt: Talikota in 1565 brought military defeat, followed by the capital's destruction, while a reduced kingdom continued under the Aravidu dynasty.

title: Battle of Talikota (1565): Defeat of Vijayanagara and the Fall of Its Capital
